items.title: Boolean circuits: basis, fan-in, size, and depth
items.strategy: Fix finite directed acyclic Boolean circuits with input nodes, constants, NOT gates, and fan-in-two AND/OR gates. Define size as the number of non-input gates and depth as the longest input-to-output gate path, while recording the constant-factor equivalence of the usual fixed finite bases.

items.title: Circuit families and P/poly
items.strategy: Define a family as one circuit for each input length, with no effectiveness requirement, and define P/poly by polynomial circuit size. Separate this nonuniform quantifier order from a single machine that constructs circuits.

items.title: Every polynomial-time language has polynomial-size circuits
items.strategy: Unroll a fixed polynomial-time computation into a layered tableau circuit. Bound the number of local-update gates and use the fixed basis conversion only after the polynomial size bound is established; no circuit-generator claim is inferred from this containment.

items.title: Polynomial advice for a deterministic machine
items.strategy: Define a length-indexed advice string a_n of polynomial length supplied to a deterministic polynomial-time machine on every n-bit input. Make explicit that advice depends only on n and need not be computable from n.

items.title: P/poly equals polynomial time with polynomial advice
items.strategy: For circuit families, encode the length-n circuit as advice and evaluate its gates in topological order. Conversely, hardwire the finitely many advice bits into a circuit simulating the advised machine, charging the advice length and the simulation separately.

items.title: Some undecidable languages have polynomial-size circuits
items.strategy: Choose an undecidable tally language U and form the binary length language L={x : 1^{|x|} is in U}. For each length n, a constant-output circuit gives the single bit U(1^n), while restricting a decider for L to inputs 1^n would decide U. This preserves undecidability without confusing nonuniform existence with an effective circuit construction.

items.title: Boolean formulas and deterministic branching programs
items.strategy: Define a formula as a rooted tree with repeated variable or constant leaves permitted, counting connective gates and constant occurrences but not variable leaves. Define a deterministic branching program as a finite acyclic query graph with bit-labelled outgoing edges and 0/1 sinks, measured by vertices.

items.title: AC0, NC1, and NC under a stated uniformity convention
items.strategy: Define AC0 using polynomial size, constant depth, and unbounded-fan-in AND/OR/NOT; define NC1 and NC using polynomial-size bounded-fan-in circuits of logarithmic and polylogarithmic depth. State within the item the logspace-uniform circuit-description convention used for the ensuing containment, without asserting it for arbitrary P/poly families.

items.title: NC1 is contained in L, and L is contained in NC2
items.strategy: Evaluate a log-depth bounded-fan-in circuit in logarithmic space by storing one O(log n)-bit child-choice path and recomputing the current gate address from the output gate whenever a value is needed; do not store a logarithmic stack of gate addresses. For the reverse inclusion, encode reachability between the polynomially many configurations of a logspace machine by repeated squaring, specify a logspace-uniform indexing scheme, and bound depth by O(log^2 n).

items.title: Counting bounded-size Boolean circuits
items.strategy: Encode each of s topologically ordered gates by its type and its at most two predecessors among n+s available wires. Multiply the choices, absorb constants, and obtain at most 2^{O(s log(n+s))} functions represented by circuits of size s.

items.title: Almost all Boolean functions require exponential circuit size
items.strategy: Compare the bounded-circuit count with the 2^{2^n} Boolean functions on n inputs. Choose a concrete c>0 so size at most c2^n/n represents a vanishing fraction, and distinguish this existential lower bound from an explicit lower-bound construction.

items.title: Circuit satisfiability
items.strategy: Define CircuitSAT for a finite encoded circuit with a designated output gate: accept exactly when some assignment to its input nodes makes that output one. Fix the encoding as a directed acyclic gate list so the certificate size and verifier are unambiguous.

items.title: CircuitSAT is NP-complete
items.strategy: Verify a guessed input assignment by evaluating the circuit in topological order. For hardness, transform a Cook--Levin formula to a circuit gate-by-gate, prove preservation of satisfiability and polynomial encoding size, and state the reduction direction explicitly.

items.title: The Karp--Lipton collapse
items.strategy: Assume NP is contained in P/poly and use SAT self-reducibility to obtain a polynomial-size circuit that outputs a satisfying assignment whenever one exists. For a Pi_2 predicate, reduce each existential tail at (x,y) to a formula f(x,y), then express membership as the existence of one polynomial-size search circuit C such that, for every y, C(f(x,y)) outputs an assignment satisfying f(x,y). The deterministic predicate checks only the displayed assignment, not the globally uncheckable claim that C decides SAT. Define PH and Sigma_2^p in the statement and conclude PH = Sigma_2^p with the hypothesis and quantifier order visible.

items.title: Polynomial-size circuits imply a uniform polynomial-time generator
items.strategy: Mark the inference false: the circuit family quantifies separately over input lengths and may encode an undecidable unary language. Identify uniform generation as an additional algorithmic requirement, not a consequence of a size bound.

items.title: Shannon counting gives an explicit circuit-hard function
items.strategy: Mark the inference false: counting proves that hard truth tables exist but supplies neither a computable description nor a way to recognise one. Contrast the cardinality argument with the separate explicit lower-bound problem.

title: Boolean Circuits and Nonuniform Complexity: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: Hardwiring a length-indexed advice string
items.strategy: For a small advised machine, replace each of its advice-bit reads by a constant gate and trace one input through the resulting circuit. Then encode the same circuit as advice and evaluate its gate list, displaying both directions of the equivalence on the same finite instance.

items.title: A Sigma_2 verification of a candidate SAT circuit
items.strategy: For a concrete Pi_2 predicate, display the existential choice of a polynomial-size SAT search circuit C followed by the universal y and the deterministic check that C(f(x,y)) is a satisfying assignment of f(x,y). Emphasize that the check verifies the supplied witness locally and never attempts to certify global agreement with satisfiability.

items.title: Unary circuits for an undecidable language are not uniformly generated
items.strategy: For an undecidable tally language U, let the circuit at length n be the constant bit indicating whether 1^n is in U, so the resulting binary length language has constant-size circuits. A uniform generator would decide U by constructing that circuit and evaluating it on 1^n.

items.title: Sharp-P and Gap-P functions
items.strategy: Define #P functions as accepting-path counts of polynomial-time nondeterministic machines and Gap-P functions as accepting minus rejecting path counts. Fix binary branching and binary output encodings as conventions, so multiplicities and signs are well defined.

items.title: NumberSAT
items.strategy: Define NumberSAT on an encoded Boolean formula with its declared variable list as the exact number of satisfying assignments. State that unused variables remain part of the declared list, preventing accidental changes to the count under an encoding rewrite.

items.title: NumberSAT belongs to Sharp-P
items.strategy: Use one nondeterministic binary choice for each declared variable and accept exactly the satisfying assignments. Give the one-to-one correspondence between computation paths and assignments, including malformed-formula rejection.

items.title: Parsimonious reductions between counting functions
items.strategy: Define a polynomial-time map f from instances of one counting problem to another to be parsimonious when the two output counts are exactly equal on every instance. Contrast this equality with ordinary decision many-one reduction in the statement.

items.title: The Cook--Levin construction can be made parsimonious
items.strategy: Use a path-bijective one-tape simulator with transition-specific intermediate states. Construct the one-hot tableau formula and its complete lexicographically ordered variable list with no auxiliary variables. Prove inverse maps between accepting tagged paths and satisfying assignments and polynomial construction time.

items.title: NumberSAT is Sharp-P-complete under parsimonious reductions
items.strategy: Combine membership with the parsimonious Cook--Levin map for an arbitrary #P machine. Keep the source machine, input, accepting-path count, formula, and its satisfying-assignment count in one equality chain.

items.title: The nonnegative function class FP
items.strategy: For this page, define FP to mean total nonnegative integer-valued functions whose binary representations are computable in deterministic polynomial time. Record this codomain convention explicitly, since arbitrary signed FP functions cannot literally be #P path counts.

items.title: FP is contained in Sharp-P
items.strategy: On input x, compute f(x) in binary and nondeterministically select one of exactly f(x) accepting branches by comparing a guessed binary integer with f(x). Account for the power-of-two padding branches and reject the excess branches.

items.title: Sharp-P is closed under sum and product
items.strategy: For sums, make a leading tagged nondeterministic choice of machine; for products, run the first machine and then independently run the second along every surviving branch. Prove the resulting accepting-path counts by finite addition and multiplication.

items.title: MajoritySAT
items.strategy: Define MajoritySAT to ask whether a formula with n declared variables has strictly more than 2^{n-1} satisfying assignments. Make the strict threshold explicit, including the n=0 convention.

items.title: PP is strict sign testing for Gap-P
items.strategy: Translate a PP machine's majority condition into the positivity of accepting paths minus rejecting paths. Conversely normalise a Gap-P witness to a common polynomial binary-branching bound and build a PP machine whose strict majority is equivalent to positive gap.

items.title: MajoritySAT is PP-complete
items.strategy: Membership guesses the declared assignment uniformly. For hardness, normalize the PP machine to exactly 2^p paths with a accepting paths, and use parsimonious Cook--Levin to obtain a formula phi on q declared variables with #phi=a, padding by forced variables so q>=p. Introduce a selector z and a polynomial-size comparison formula T on those q variables with exactly 2^q-2^{p-1} satisfying assignments; then theta=(not z and phi) or (z and T) has a+2^q-2^{p-1} satisfying assignments out of 2^{q+1}, which is a strict majority exactly when a>2^{p-1}.

items.title: PP is closed under complement
items.strategy: If L={x:g(x)>0} for an integer-valued Gap-P function g, then its complement is {x:g(x)<=0}={x:1-g(x)>0}. Show directly that Gap-P is closed under negation and addition of the constant-one gap, then apply strict sign testing; the offset handles the zero case exactly.

items.title: Polynomial time with a Sharp-P oracle
items.strategy: Define P^#P using an oracle that returns the binary value of a fixed #P function on each query, with polynomial query length and polynomially many adaptive queries. Distinguish this function oracle from a yes/no language oracle.

items.title: NP is contained in P with a Sharp-P oracle
items.strategy: For a language in NP, use the #P function counting accepting verifier witnesses and query whether its returned integer is positive. Alternatively route through the parsimonious NumberSAT construction; state why exact binary output permits the zero test in polynomial time.

items.title: Sharp-P is a language class
items.strategy: Mark the statement false under the page convention: #P members map inputs to nonnegative integers, whereas a language has Boolean membership. Use NumberSAT to exhibit the categorical mismatch and name its associated decision language separately.

items.title: Every decision many-one reduction is parsimonious
items.strategy: Mark the statement false by adding a fresh unused variable to a SAT formula: satisfiability is preserved by a polynomial-time many-one map while the satisfying-assignment count doubles. Contrast decision preservation with exact count preservation.

title: Counting Complexity and Sharp-P: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: A two-branch computation and its parsimonious tableau formula
items.strategy: Display a machine with two accepting paths, identify the two legal tableaux, and show that the selected exact tableau encoding has exactly two satisfying assignments. Point out which auxiliary-variable convention preserves uniqueness.

items.title: Deciding satisfiability by a NumberSAT oracle query
items.strategy: Query the exact NumberSAT value of a small formula and decide satisfiability by testing whether the returned binary integer is nonzero. Contrast that one query with the exponentially many assignments it summarizes.

items.title: NumberSAT is not a Boolean membership predicate
items.strategy: Evaluate NumberSAT on two formulas with different positive counts and observe that neither output is a truth value. The associated SAT language records only whether the count is nonzero, so it is a different object.
